subsubtopic: FOOD SERVICE INDUSTRY-SHORTAGE OF SKILLED WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the restaurant and food service industry has become a large and dynamic sector of the Canadian economy with sales of $15 billion, or 4.5 per cent of Canada's GNP, and 600,000 employees, or 5.7 per cent of the national labour force. In addition, it earned $1 billion in foreign exchange last year from visiting tourists.
In 1982, a recession year, employment in the food service industry actually increased by 2,000 jobs. When one considers the unemployment situation in Canada, surely the service industries are part of the solution, and the largest sector, the food service industry, deserves encouragement for job creation and business growth.
At present the industry lacks the schools and standards necessary to educate the skilled technicians who make this industry grow. Our colleges graduate good cooks but not world-class chefs.
This shortage of skilled trades is becoming a major bottleneck in the expansion of this industry, and it is an area where the Government can help by upgrading training facilities and by designating some of the food service trades as national occupations under the National Training Act.
In addition, consideration must also be given to revising the tax system to stimulate these labour intensive industries.

subsubtopic: POTENTIAL JOB CREATION OF ERIE CONSTITUENCY PROJECTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is no shortage of work to be done in Canada. As well, there is no shortage of willing labour. All that is required is the funding and organization. 1 believe these are some of the reasons we have a Department of Employment and Immigration. I would like to suggest to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) that plans exist for many long term projects involving conservation and improvement of transportation facilities which would keep many people employed for a long time.
In my constituency of Erie two such projects have been on the drawing board for many, many months. These are very worth-while endeavours involving flood control in the City of Port Colborne, and modifications to the old Welland Canal to accommodate mooring of ships. The total cost of these two projects is roughly $9 million.
If the current administration were willing to sponsor either or both of these projects, which would cost but a small fraction of the $1.5 billion bailout of Canadair, the benefits to the environment and the local economy would be tremendous. Federal funding would be put to good use in assisting with these projects, especially in light of the fact that over $5 million was granted in the neighbouring constituency for creating parks and doing landscaping.

subsubtopic: LETTERS SUPPORTING RETENTION OF CROWSNEST PASS RATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his Government 1,500 letters individually signed by residents of the Prince Albert area, who ask for Crow rate retention. These letters, which are addressed to the Prime Minister, were gathered by the Prince Albert Chamber of Commerce and reflect broad based public opinion which continues to support retention of the Crow rate.
These 1,500 letters, together with 3,400 petition signatures and 2,100 signed endorsements of the New Democratic Party's Crow retention policy, add up to an extremely significant statement of public opinion. I will send these letters across to the Prime Minister and I ask him to answer my written question involving public representation of the Crow retention.
A similar question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) produced 38,713 signatures favouring Crow retention, and only 69 for Crow change. That is a 99.8 per cent vote in favour of Crow retention. This kind of public response clearly demonstrates why New Democrats continue to oppose Bill C-155 and propose an alternative policy which will upgrade the railways and keep the Crow rate for western farmers. We want to ensure that western voices are heard by the committee on transport, and we urge that the committee travel throughout the West in its examination of Bill C-155. I have those letters here in my hand, Madam Speaker.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR PROPOSED BAN ON SMOKING IN AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, some two weeks ago I made representation to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) with regard to the possibility of having a partial or complete ban on smoking in all aircraft whose flights originate in Canada. My colleagues will be interested to know that since that time I have received over 150 letters. Just this morning I received support for that proposal from one group which spoke for 34,000 Canadians.
1 realized that my colleague, the Member of Parliament for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail), asked a question yesterday. I believe the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott) also brought this to our attention. The purpose of my statement is to encourage Hon. Members, and to say that if they are also getting this kind of response for a ban such as this, perhaps we should be moving to institute such a ban, in view of the fact that it is for the safety of Canadians in the first instance, while also adding to the comfort of people who are travelling. 1 encourage those who hear me to write to me, to my colleague from Restigouche, or to the Hon. subsubtopic: CELEBRATION OF FOUR HUNDREDTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, according to our rules the House does not sit tomorrow as we celebrate St. Jean Baptiste day to honour one of the two founding peoples of Canada.
I wish to bring to the attention of the House the fact that tomorrow is also an important holiday for Newfoundland. June 24 is Discovery Day in Newfoundland, and it is especially significant this year as Newfoundland celebrates its four hundredth anniversary.
On August 5, 1583, Sir Humphrey Gilbert read a proclamation in St. John's, which was then a settled community, formally claiming sovereignty in the name of Queen Elizabeth I, and thereby establishing Britain's first colony. Today, her direct descendant, Prince Charles, and the Princess of Wales, are in St. John's to inaugurate the four hundredth anniversary celebrations officially.
1 am pleased to bring this national historic event to the attention of the House in the absence of my colleagues from St. John's East and St. John's West who are in St. John's to participate in the official ceremonies. I am sure all Hon. Members will want to join me in saluting the proud people of Newfoundland on the occasion of their four hundredth anniversary.

subsubtopic: VANCOUVER COMMENTATOR'S VIEWS OF MEDIA WATCH GROUP
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, recently a commentator on CKVU-TV in Vancouver topped his own reputation for promoting poisonous prejudice by stating, "It is my hope that Media Watch and its army of snoops will be found in the front lines where they can be raped by the Russians." I am sure that all Hon. Members of Parliament abhor such an obscene statement from a professional broadcaster on a station which is licensed by the CRTC.
Media Watch is dedicated to informing the public on issues surrounding the portrayal of women in the media and the detrimental effects of sex role stereotyping and pornography. This incident shows the need for such a service.
CKVU-TV, by refusing to apologize or demand a retraction from its commentator, has condoned hatred and violence against women generally. Media Watch appropriately refused an opportunity to rebut on CKVU because "the question of whether or not women should be raped by an invading army is not debatable."
As in the case of First Choice Pay TV, the CKVU incident makes a mockery of the unenforceable human rights policy of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters. Since the broadcasting industry is not policing itself, legislative action is imperative. I urge the Government and the House to give priority to the Private Members' Bill proposed by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), which would amend the Broadcasting Act to prohibit such abusive comments.

subsubtopic: FUNDS REQUIRED FOR NATIONAL MEETING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, almost all Members of the House will be aware of the important work of the Block Parent Program. From its humble beginnings in London, Ontario, in the Fall of 1968, the Block Parent Program has grown to the point where it now encompasses 800 plus communities of all sizes. There are Block Parent communities in all ten Provinces and in both Territories. All of the 800 plus Block Parent communities in the national Block Parent Program use the same national symbol and house sign, thus enabling children to move from one coast of Canada to the other and still find their sign of safety, the national Block Parent house sign, in windows of houses in their new communities.
The Block Parent Program has provided a service of untold value to lost or frigthened children and their families throughout Canada. However, there is some concern that national Block Parent communication needs to be strengthened through a national advisory committee and the opportunity for Block
June 23, 1983

Parent organizations from the various regions of Canada to meet face to face in personal dialogue. Toward that end a national Block Parent advisory committee meeting has been proposed for October of this year. The cost of such a meeting would be $7,000, a small price for a meeting of such an important national organization, but one which its voluntary members will find difficult to raise. In the interest of preserving the national Block Parent Program and its important work, I would hope that the federal Government, perhaps through the Solicitor General's Department, can provide some financial assistance to bring a national meeting to fruition.

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. I would like to congratulate him for being so elegantly dressed today in his blue conservative jacket. His recovery is obviously well under way.
A group of Members of Parliament met recently with some Canadian and American Congressmen and Senators. We were told that the Americans were not going to get their deficit down and that all the Congressmen had other priorities, the Democrats with social programs, the Republicans with defence programs, and that there would be no compromise. Therefore the American deficit would continue and we would have upcoming high interest rates. This is a very serious matter for the Canadian economy. Would the Minister tell the House what steps he recommended to Cabinet, or he is prepared to take, to prepare against this eventuality, that is, to make our interest rates independent of American ones? Is he now prepared to bring down Canadian interest rates so that we will have some real sustained recovery as we all want?

subsubtopic: LEVEL OF INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will not pass any comment on the blue shirt worn by my colleague, but I will address the more serious aspect of his question.
I should like to remind him that today interest rates on Treasury bills and on Government bonds extending up to seven years are lower than American rates. My hon. friend remembers that over the last two years there were times when Canadian rates were up to 5 per cent and 6 per cent above American rates. We have pursued a very appropriate monetary and fiscal policy. We are seeing the very beneficial effects of that policy at the present time in terms of lower inflation, a high rate of growth, and interest rates that are now even lower
than the American ones. All of this is taking place while we enjoy a stable dollar.
I think the policies the Government has followed in the last year and a half have certainly been appropriate for the situation I hope that for the rest of this year and also in 1984 the Canadian people will reap the benefits of all the sacrifices which all of us have been asked to carry in the last year.

Madam Speaker, as a supplementary question let me ask the Minister about the benefits people are reaping. Supposedly we have a recovery, about which the Minister has been crowing in the House of Commons. Would he agree that we have high rates of unemployment, that he has been going around the country attacking consumers because his budget will put a lot of taxes on them later, and that he has been attacking labour, because he is now speaking of wage controls?
I would like to know what are the Minister's policies. Will we face another six and five, say a four and three program? What does the Minister mean when he attacks labour, and wage increases? What will he do to lower the rate of unemployment? We cannot have a recovery if we still have so many unemployed people in the country. This is a profits recovery, not a people recovery.

Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague has some very strange information sources. I would remind him that not only were we successful in bringing down inflation to 5.4 per cent this May, compared to last year, but since 1982, we have also managed to create about 330,000 new or additional jobs in Canada. Employment has been rising regularly and consistently during the last six months, and during the last two, we were able to bring the unemployment rate down from 12.8 percent to 12.4 per cent. The unemployment rate is still very high, too high, and we must keep on trying to bring unemployment down. In any case, we shall be successful in doing so if we bring down inflation, which will keep our interest rates at a fairly low level, and our prices competitive on world markets. When I criticized certain wage settlements, one in particular, I was not criticizing the workers or union leaders specifically. I merely said that employers and workers, or rather their union leaders, has not acted responsibly.
I am happy to see that at the present time, collective bargaining agreements are being negotiated in a very responsible manner, since the average wage settlement amounts to about 6.5 per cent in the private sector, if we exclude the construction industry. However, we shall have to try and avoid situations in the construction industry that would touch off another inflationary spiral, which would affect the workers themselves first of all.

speechtext: Does South Korea prohibit the importation of footwear or clothing from Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subsubtopic: SOUTH KOREA-IMPORT RESTRICTIONS
speechtext:
Imports of footwear and clothing into Korea from all countries, including Canada, are not absolutely prohibited. In the case of footwear, imports are not restricted, i.e. import licences are automatically approved, but the general tariff is 50 per cent. One exception is women's dress shoes, which, though granted automatic import licence approval, are under surveillance. However, it is likely that this item will receive full automatic approval status this year.
In the case of clothing, of a total 217 tariff items, 142 items are restricted under the Annual Trade Plan and a further 34 under other Special Laws. The remaining 41 items or 18.9 per cent are automatically issued import licences. In addition, the general tariff rate on all clothing is 50 per cent.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (York East) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO CHANGE NAME OF ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-663, to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased to be able to proceed this afternoon with my Private Members' Bill. It is a rather simple Bill and I hope the House will give it expeditious approval.
In summary, Bill C-663 seeks to amend the Old Age Security Act and to change the title of that Act to read the "Senior
June 23, 1983

Citizens Benefit Act". The reason I am proposing this elimination of the words "old age" is that they do imply that at age 65 a person is no longer capable of leading a productive life or making a valuable contribution to society.
The reason I bring this matter before the House today stems from the fact that the constituency which I represent in Metropolitan Toronto has, I believe, the highest number of senior citizens of any constituency in that area, and has probably one of the highest numbers in the country. I am sure, along with places such as Victoria, the area of York East, comprising the Borough of East York and the "old town" of Don Mills, as we call it, has one of the highest numbers of senior citizens in the country.
Tomorrow on my birthday I will become a certain age. I do not believe that the passage of time has diminished my effectiveness just because I turned a certain age. And I am sure that just because someone reaches the age of 65, their ability or effectiveness is not diminished. In my constituency, Mr. Speaker, we have a large number of senior citizen groups who perform a range of community activities and tasks. This group meets almost incessantly, whether for a legitimate community activity such as the raising of funds for worthy projects, to work on handicrafts, or for lawn bowling, to play euchre or bridge and participate in other forms of recreation. Indeed, up until recently many members of the Borough of East York Council were people approaching or over the age of 65, although that has changed somewhat in the last few years. In my constituency, however, senior citizens continue to take a leading role through church and community organizations.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, the population of senior citizens is rapidly increasing due to a number of factors, not the least of which is that married couples today are choosing to have fewer children. With medical advances, we have noted that the life expectancy for Canadians has increased dramatically over the last few years. I do not have the actual figures but I believe the life expectancy for a man in this country is about 70 years and for a women it is about 75 years. As we come out of the current recession and embark on a new era of economic growth based on high technology industries in which Canada has a leading edge, it is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that, notwithstanding all the gloomy forecasts which one reads in the press, there will indeed be a labour shortage as the years go by.
One way, of course, to deal with that, as Canada has dealt with it traditionally, is through immigration. However, there is a debate as to whether or not Canada should be taking skilled people from the underdeveloped countries. Perhaps these people should be staying in their own countries to develop the economies there. Of course, we can take large numbers of unskilled workers, and we have done that I am happy to say over the years. However, it seems to me that with new opportunities for growth and labour shortage demands, especially in skilled trades, it would be worth while if we encouraged the
Old Age Security Act
private sector, certainly the Public Service, to keep people on the job past the age of 65.
If the medical advances which I have cited are correct, then it stands to reason that people are just as agile at the age of 69 as they were at the age of 65. I note, for example, our colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has toiled many years in the House, is over the age of 65. He has made and continues to make a very effective contribution to the House of Commons. He has certainly set an example for those of us who are many years his junior.
The former Member for Spadina in the 1940s and 1950s, now in the Senate, Senator David Croll, is one of those life senators who at the age of 83 still comes to the caucus every Wednesday. In fact, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail), will testify, Senator Croll made a very lucid intervention this week at our national Liberal caucus. He is a gentleman who undertakes speaking engagements at the age of 83 and chaired an all-party Senate committee a few years ago at which time he issued a very laudable and worth-while report entitled "Retirement Without Tears". If one opens that report one finds a quotation from Psalms 71:9, and I quote:
Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth.
One of the recommendations in his report is that the mandatory retirement age be abolished. It has been contended by a number of people-and I would lean towards this interpretation myself-that with the recent enactment and entrenchment of the Charter of Rights, a mandatory retirement age provision of 65 may be proven to be unconstitutional.
I have been rather active in the last year or so in fighting the post office on behalf of one of its employees. I have many constituents in my riding who work at the central postal facility. This gentleman, who was doing a manual job and performing it very well, had no performance problems and a good work record, had to retire at the age of 65 when he was clearly capable of carrying on his particular tasks. We fought that case through the Canadian Human Rights Commission and we received a "stay of execution" for this particular gentleman. However, he was forced to retire this year at the age of 66. Post office officials admit that there was no appreciable difference in his performance at the age of 66 from what it was the day before his sixty-fifth birthday.
Obviously, we cannot make a carte blanche statement that all persons over the age of 65 are of sound mind and body and that they can perform the tasks of younger people. Equally, however, we cannot say that people who have reached the age of 60 years can do the same kind of work. In my submission, a retirement age of 65 is completely and utterly arbitrary and should be changed. In fact, one of the recommendations of Senator Croll's committee was, of course, to abolish this mandatory age for retirement. One of the arguments which was used is quoted on page 51 of the report:
Finally, the increasing burden of the older dependent population should be reduced by the elimination of mandatory retirement at age 65. The new environment which is envisaged for the mid-1980s on-with demand for labour

June 23, 1983
Old Age Security Act
high and age discrimination abolished-should result in the increased participation of older workers in the labour force. As a result of this increased participation, more goods and services will be produced to support those of the older population who are not working.
The report then goes on to state its conclusions. Put quite simply, Mr. Speaker-and this is as a result of representations 1 have received from a number of my constituents-it is felt that the words "old age" are somewhat derogatory. Really, when one thinks of old age, one thinks in Keynesian terms. I feel that when one uses the term "old age this" and "old age that", it really conjures un memories of the workhouses, the alms houses, and of another era which is long gone. Today, as we see in our own House of Commons, in the Senate and through our society, because of medical advances and improved social conditions, people are living longer, making more productive use of their lives and their skills, and certainly should be utilized by society.
This change, if enacted, will not cost the Government anything; it can be done simply by a stroke of the pen. I have been led to believe that the Government has some reservations about making this change on the argument that the whole pension system is being studied by a committee of this House. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the enactment of this change, as 1 have proposed, will in no way undermine that particular study now being conducted by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith).
In conclusion, I take great pleasure in bringing this Bill forward. I am sure by the rapt attention I have received from Hon. Members that they are of one mind and will allow the Bill to go to committee. Hence we will have rapid passage and end this blatant discrimination, in a sense semantic discrimination, in one of our statutes. Henceforth when someone receives one's pension at the appropriate time in the month, one will not be receiving an old age pension; one will be receiving a senior citizen's benefit.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO CHANGE NAME OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not surprised that this particular issue was raised by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Collenette) because of his well known concern not just for senior citizens but for people. This has been very evident throughout his career as a Member of Parliament. I am sure that when he went through the legislation and saw something which struck a negative cord in his mind about the meaning or the semantic implication of words such as "old age", it was only a short time thereafter that he saw fit to draft a Bill and fortunately got it on the list for discussion today.
When we are considering this kind of Bill in Private Members' Hour, we are provided with an opportunity to be reminded of the need for additional help to senior citizens. All too often there is a tendency to think that we have done about all we could possibly do and that there is no crying need out there for anything other than possibly more money. Innovative governments have indicated areas where senior citizens have fallen short financially either because pensions were not in existence during the 1930s and 1940s or because their pensions were so small or not indexed that inflation has eaten away at
them to the point where they must go out and seek employment, despite the fact that they cannot draw unemployment insurance and are not protected under provincial workmen's compensation plans. Out of sheer necessity such senior citizens have had to go out to work.
Governments of various political stripes have seen fit to get together and provide benefits, such as senior citizens not having to pay OHIP premiums. In other areas assistance is given in the form of cheaper hair cuts, free bus rides and things of that nature. At the federal Government level low rental housing units have been provided for senior citizens. It is hard to imagine that prior to 1968 some initiative had not been taken in this particular way because it has been such a successful program and has met a particular need of senior citizens.
A Bill such as this one reminds us of the fact that we must constantly look for the opportunity to come up with ways and means for Canadian taxpayers to help the people who made the country what it is today, the people who gave of their time, their effort and their skills to see to it that Canada became one of the great nations of the world. I would remind people who have a tendency to knock this country that when I held a portfolio in Immigration, in those particular days and even now somewhere between 700,000 and 900,000 people per year applied to come to Canada because they saw it as a great and wonderful place in which to live and, more important, where they would receive decent treatment. We have often heard that a country is judged by the way it treats its senior citizens or people in need. Senior citizens are the people who gave the image and character that we know as Canada today.
I was a little surprised when I heard a stage whisper across the way that this was only a frill, that it just changed the name. I suggest with respect that it is more than that. It is an indication that we are trying to remove, as we do with women's issues, any chauvinistic implication of legislation. It is appropriate that the Hon. Member for York East is trying to do what he can to give a better impact to a Bill of this nature, particularly by the name change.
It is not unusual that this kind of thing takes place in Private Members' Hour. If we want to recommend anything in this particular place, it costs money. We must do it in the form of a motion, whereas in Private Members' Hour we are pretty well confined. We have to be innovative and find ways and means for Private Members to right what is perceived as a wrong or to correct something which gives the wrong indication. For example, Canada Mortgage and Housing was once known as Central Mortgage and Housing. The idea of "Canada" being in the name rather than "Central" points to the impact of the symbolism of using the name Canada.
I believe it was the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) when he was a Private Member who brought in a Bill to change the name of TransCanada Airlines to Air Canada. We have seen things such as the Dominion Bureau of Statistics being changed to Statistics Canada because it has a more solid and better image of what that Department is all about. We had a recent indication of how a
June 23, 1983

Private Member could significantly change the country's history when the name Dominion Day was changed to Canada Day, much to the pleasure of the majority of Canadians, although they might not have like the method of accomplishing it. When we have tried 347 other ways of getting this done and finally come up with a solution on a Friday afternoon, I think it is one of the better things we have done here in Private Members' Hour.
Also I remember that when Father Sean O'Sullivan was here he was checking around and discovered that there was nothing to indicate that the beaver was the Canadian symbol. Through a Private Member's Bill action was taken. It may seem a frill or it may seem unimportant, but it is one more indication of the thoughtfulness of people who want to move in this particular way to make such a change.
When I began my remarks I said that we were being given an opportunity to talk about our senior citizens. All too often we talk about two million people over the age of 65 and have a tendency to get lost in the numbers rather than deal with individual needs. There are many senior citizens, single pensioners or others, who for one reason or another-quite often through no fault of their own-miss out on the Canada Pension Plan or on an old age pension.
Because we are talking about senior citizens and the proposed name changes, I want to highlight the story of a Royal Canadian Air Force veteran who was 27 years of age when he enlisted. He won his wings at Summerside, Prince Edward Island. He rose to the rank of Warrant Officer First-Class. He was given a Spitfire and he wheeled it over Great Britain and France, as Rod Goodman indicated in his article which appeared in the Sunday Star on June 19. He pointed out that this man's war service for Canada ended when his right leg was crushed. He spent a year in British Hospitals undergoing bone transplants to save the leg; his kneecap was removed. His Spitfire was shot down by a cannon from a German fighter just off the English coast in 1943.
As Mr. Goodman indicated, this grateful country welcomed him home. He returned to his job in a meat packing plant but it was no good because his leg would not function in the cold. He decided to start his own business. While his wife worked in an insurance compensation department, he helped found the Metro Cab Company. The climate continued to torture him. The significant part of the story is that finally a doctor from the Department of Veterans Affairs-he was not one of Mr. Wright's own physicians whom he could have set up to do this-told him that he could expect pain to be his constant companion unless he moved to a warmer climate. In the spring of 1952, just before turning the age of 38, Mr. Wright and his wife moved to California. They did what they could there, working in various ways to maintain their income. They returned each year to visit his aging mother until her death four years ago.
The Wrights now live in Escondido, California. Mr. Wright thought that he should at least be entitled to a partial old age pension. He had been paying into the United States social security system and was receiving a small pension that did not
Old Age Security Act
help ends meet. This spring, at age 69, he applied for a partial Canadian Government old age pension; he was turned down.
What are the criteria? The regional director of pensions in Toronto says that an applicant outside Canada may qualify for a partial monthly pension provided he or she was a Canadian citizen or a legal resident of Canada on the day preceding the day he or she ceased to reside in Canada. Mr. Wright qualified on that score, but he was defeated by the second stipulation that he or she reside in Canada at least 20 full years after attaining the age of 18.
We know why that specific requirement was put into the Act. However, this war veteran who was shot down, who endeavoured to do what he could to maintain himself in Canada, who was told by a Veterans Affairs doctor that he had to move to a southern climate, is not applying for a full pension but asking for a partial old age pension.
Here is the tragic part of the whole matter. Mr. Wright qualified on the ground that he had been a Canadian citizen when he left the country, but he was defeated by the second stipulation that he or she reside in Canada 20 full years. Because a war injury forced him to a southern climate when it did, Mr. Wright fell 60 days short of help from the Canadian Government.
Mr. Goodman asks, was it fair? I do not think it was fair. I have already brought this to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell). I asked for his help in endeavouring to convince the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) that there must be some way to find a discretionary way of giving this former Royal Canadian Air Force officer, this veteran, some help with his pension when he so desperately needs it.
This is the kind of matter we can highlight in the Bill such as this. It indicates that people like Mr. Wright are part of the two million who seem to fall between the chairs of the legislation. I do not think anyone in Canada really feels that Mr. Wright is not entitled to some form of pension. It is typical of Mr. Wright that he did not ask for the full pension but for a partial pension, because he had paid into social security in the United States. I will keep pressing this issue, as other Members press issues involving senior citizens.
There are two concerns. The Hon. Member for York East indicated that the Government was not very keen on this move because pensions, and all that sort of thing, are being discussed at the present time. I do not know what the Government is thinking or whether it would contemplate raising that argument in this debate.
There are two matters that concern me. The first is whether the demand for the name change is as widespread as is indicated here, given the fact that money will have to be spent in order to make that change. their cheque, no matter what the name is at the top of the cheque.
1 think that given the choice, most pensioners would prefer to see the significant funds associated with implementing a program name change directed instead to the pockets of their less fortunate peers. Do pensioners really want us spending taxpayers' dollars on devising and publicizing a new name and seeing its implementation through? 1 do not know that that is really what they anticipate or are looking for when they look to Government.
What I would like to see as our first social priority is to raise the level of the guaranteed income supplement payable to single pensioners. This was stated in the federal Government's green paper on pension reform, "Better Pensions for Canadians". The necessary funds are not available as yet. I like the "as yet" because it gives the impression that that issue as raised in the green paper is something that will be implemented by the Government. The money is not available as yet. Lest people think there is a niggardly amount of money being spent in this area, we should point out that the taxpayers of Canada contribute $8 billion annually for assistance, cheques and moneys of one kind or another for our senior citizens.
1 heard a stage whisper earlier that this might be considered a frill rather than something significant that we should be doing. I do not consider it that way. I feel it is a good move by a Member who has a real concern about the impact of the negative response that one gets from the idea of old age. Old age connotes to all of us individuals passionately and desperately in need of help, unable to look after themselves and requiring assistance of one kind or another. I think the suggestion of using the term "senior citizens" is more appropriate. I hope that one day the Act will be changed in that way, if this Bill does not go to committee as a result of this debate.
We have a tendency when using the words "old age" to think, unhappily, in a negative way. Those who have taken the time, and that is probably true of all Members of Parliament, have been very much impressed with the many organizations that pensioners and older Canadians have formed in recent years, in part to present their views to Governments on various issues affecting them. I do not know whether they have made a representation with respect to this name. If not, I am sure it will be added to their list, as it should be.
These groups have a long list of accomplishments. Right now many are involved in preparing submissions and presentations to the parliamentary task force on pension reform, referred to by the Hon. Member for York East. Two such organizations have already had the opportunity to appear before the task force, the Council on Pension Reform for Singles and the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation. The focus of their presentations was how to improve our pension system to provide better benefits for older Canadians, both now and in the future.
Among the recommendations of the Council on Pension Reform for Singles was a suggestion that the income guarantee to single pensioners be raised at least to the poverty line and then additionally increased to compensate those singles born too soon to participate in the Canada Pension Plan. The
Council also suggested that a death benefit similar to that payable to a Canada Pension Plan contributor's estate be made available under the Old Age Security Program on behalf of these same single pensioners. Other recommendations concern the provision of larger tax exemptions for single pensioners and payment of Old Age Security at age 60 to single pensioners looking after aged parents or those forced to retire due to disability or poor health.
What is significant about all these studies is that when people join these organizations and bring forth these studies, they have a tendency to focus on the areas where they know the need to be rather than what you or I, Mr. Speaker, perceive the need to be.
The National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation propose, among other things, continued payment of OAS-GIS for six months to the surviving spouse of a deceased pensioner, quarterly indexation of Canada Pension Plan benefits, payment of OAS-GIS at age 55 to widows of disabled pensioners and a gradual lowering of the eligibility age for pension benefits to age 60.
If this is any indication of what the task force can expect to hear from other organizations representing pensioners, and I expect that it is, financial security for pensioners is their main concern, and I underline "main". If we lived in an unreal world where money was no object, these pensioner organizations might have suggested to the parliamentary task force that the Government consider a new name for the Old Age Security Program. However, pensioners are practical people. They know only too well what the real problems are of getting by from day to day.
I do not want to speak any longer on this Bill other than to say that I would endorse the change. If it does not come about as a result of this debate or a vote on this Bill, I expect it will be one of the changes that will come about in the not too distant future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regardless of the remarks we just heard from the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Kilgour), I am very pleased to address a few remarks to Bill C-663, introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Collenette). For the record, Mr. Speaker, I should like to state that I have not been assigned any "dirty task" in talking the Bill out. I am sure that many Members in the Chamber would welcome the opportunity to give their views on the Bill.
I think it is rather interesting that the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona was embarrassed into making remarks on behalf of the Loyal Opposition. Just a few minutes ago he stood to ask that we move to the next item of business. Obviously at that time he had no care or concern about matters relating to senior citizens. When the Hon. Member for York East rose on a point of order, then the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona felt his neck and had to say a few words regarding the plight of senior citizens and recipients of the old age pension. In a very partisan way he attacked the concerns that all of us have regarding Parliament and the Government of the day. I think we must take his remarks lightly as obviously he has very little concern and care for this particular Bill.
This Bill proposes to change the name of the Old Age Security Act to the "Senior Citizens Benefits Act". The basis given for this proposal is the contention that the words "old age" imply that at age 65 a person is no longer capable of leading a productive life or making a valuable contribution to society. Certainly the name "Old Age Security Program" was never intended to carry such a negative connotation.
The current Old Age Security pension-one of three benefits provided under the Old Age Security Act-is paid to
everyone at age 65 who meets the necessary residence requirements in Canada. Eligibility for this pension is not dependent on labour force participation. You neither have to participate in the paid labour force prior to age 65, nor do you have to leave the labour force after age 65.
Persons 65 years of age and older are definitely not considered incapable of leading a productive life or making a valuable contribution to society. However, it is felt that these persons, in recognition of the number of years they have spent making Canada a better place in which to live, should have the right, if they so choose, to take life more easily, retire from the labour force, or pursue other interests and hobbies. To do this they must have an assured source of basic income and that is exactly what the Old Age Security Program is designed for.
Therefore, since the intent of the Old Age Security Program is to reward older individuals for past services to Canada and not to pay off individuals at age 65 because we do not believe they are capable of being valuable members of our society, I am sure Hon. Members will agree that the program title should not be viewed in a negative way.
If it is decided to change the name of the Old Age Security Program, however, surely it is important to choose a name that improves the current title. Care must be taken to ensure that any new name has none of the negative connotations this Private Member's Bill attributes to the phrase "old age". At the same time there are some very positive aspects of the current title that must be maintained.
In Canada, the phrase "old age" has been part of the title of income support programs for older Canadians for more than 55 years, since the introduction of the Old Age Pensions Act in 1927. The almost perfect take-up rate for the Old Age Security pension signifies that people readily identify with this federal program; they know what the program is, what it provides, and where to apply.
It is important that any new program name be acceptable to pensioners and that it identify the program as well as the current name. Clearly this is a difficult task since "old age pension" is a term with widely understood meaning. In fact, these terms have become an integral part of Canadians' pension vocabulary. Regardless of any new names we might want to attach to it, I venture to guess that most people would continue to think of it simply as their old age pension. As well, it is possible that a change in the Old Age Seucrity Program name might cause confusion among pensioners who have grown accustomed to receiving the monthly Old Age Security pension. We would have to ensure that every effort be made to make the transition as easy and as understandable as possible.
While it is not essential that any new title give more than a general understanding of the nature of the program, it is assumed that a title which gives a more accurate description of the program objectives, source of the benefits, limitations, et cetera, would be more effective than a more neutral title. As well, words or phrases which could mislead the public about the nature of the program should, as much as possible, be avoided.
June 23, 1983

The title proposed in this Bill is Senior Citizens Benefits Act. While the phrase "senior citizen" has come to be widely used when referring to older individuals, it is often used to denote those persons who are retired. Since eligibility for the Old Age Security pension is not limited to retired persons over the age of 65, "senior citizen", with respect, could be misleading. As well, the number of years of residence in Canada are used to determine who over age 65 is eligible for the pension. The word "citizen" might tend to give the false impression that an individual has to be a Canadian citizen and not just have been resident in Canada. I also want to point out that there are individuals who have stated that they consider the term "senior citizen" to be as objectionable as the term "old age".
Thus, while it may be considered desirable to change the name of the Old Age Security Program, I do not believe that Senior Citizens Benefits Act would be an appropriate choice.
What, then, would be an acceptable title? How would we find out what individuals want? When should this change take place? Of those questions, I consider the "when" to be the most important. I know that with the necessary consultation and research, an appropriate new title could be found for the Old Age Security Act. Nevertheless, we must face the fact that changing the name of the Old Age Security Program is not going to be an inexpensive procedure. There is, of course, the cost associated with finding a new name, whether it be through a general survey of our current pensioners or through some other vehicle such as the Gallup poll. However, the greatest proportion of the expense would come after the fact. An extensive advertising campaign would be required in order to minimize the confusion and concern that a name change could be expected to cause. In addition, new application forms, program information booklets, ID cards, stationery and building signage would be required.
Is our current economic situation conducive to such a change? The current economic restraint program has, as with all Canadians, had its effect on our pensioner population. This session of Parliament has seen the adoption of Bill C-131(2), which amended the Old Age Security Act. Through passage of this piece of legislation we asked all Old Age Security pensioners who could afford to do so to accept limits on the amount of indexation they would receive on their basic Old Age Security pension in 1983 and 1984. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that they accepted that challenge with a great deal of grace and have worked along those lines. While inflation has been substantially reduced and the effects of the limited indexation are minimal thus far, the program will stay in effect until the end of December, 1984.
In addition, the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) in his remarks mentioned the green paper on pension reform. As stated in that green paper, improving the financial situation of low-income, single pensioners is an urgent and pressing necessity. This vulnerable group of Canadians is not yet guaranteed an adequate income with which to make ends
Business of the House
meet, and must be assisted as soon as financial resources permit.
Therefore, even if we all agree that changing the name of the Old Age Security Program is a desirable step, I think we must carefully consider where it lies in our list of social priorities. I firmly believe, Mr. Speaker, that the people of this country understand and recognize the difficult situation facing many of their compatriots, whether it be the young, the unemployed or older, retired members of our society. 1 feel certain they would want us to expend our efforts and resources to ensure these groups receive the financial assistance they require.
While I congratulate the Hon. Member for York East on bringing this matter to our attention-it has given him the opportunity, of course, to express his views and concerns for our senior citizens and retired people-I think that at this particular time we should not consider undertaking expensive initiatives such as those suggested in this Bill.

I refer to the fact that as the law now stands, a woman between ages 60 and 65 can receive a pension payment provided she is married to someone who is 65 and over who is receipt of the pension. However, in the case of persons who are single and between the ages of 60 and 65, there is no such provision.

Mr. Speaker, it will just take the one or two minutes remaining to make a point that 1 had made a few years ago concerning adequate protection for seniors. Of course, I want to joint other Hon. Members in congratulating the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Collenette) for bringing forward this important subject today.
Some years ago I introduced a proposal to give some relief to our seniors and those who have no other visible means of support or ability to earn income in excess of $15,000 per year, or a round figure of $ 12,000 per year. I suggested that they not be forced or called upon to pay income tax; nor should they

June 23, 1983
Canada Evidence Act
have to bear the burden of filing income tax returns. Therefore, when we are speaking of pensions and our concern for seniors in Canada, I feel it is undue and unnecessary for men and women who have attained their retirement years to carry this extra burden of filing income tax forms.
Through this opportunity to intervene this afternoon, I hope 1 can focus the Government's attention once again on my proposal made a few years ago that there be a system to identify these men and women who have attained the age of retirement so that they are not forced or called upon to file these forms. For some of them, it would be a burden to pay the cost of assistance in completing these forms when, indeed, their incomes are fixed at, say, $12,000 per year or $1,000 per month. They are obviously not in the position to carry the burden of these extra costs, and it is a hardship. The Government should consider that in a civilized society this is an assistance that we could very well provide to these people in a true liberal sense.
I do thank the Hon. Member for York East for showing his concern for seniors and his understanding of what a civilized society should do in protecting our elderly, our seniors. I feel that the content of the Bill is very worth while. I do hope that by once again focusing on the matter this afternoon, the appropriate Ministers, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres), will consider my proposal to find some ways and means of eliminating, for the benefit of men and women who are in this stage of retirement in life, the unnecessary burden of filing income tax forms.
