subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Canada Evidence Act to implement the recommendations of the McDonald Commission concerning the admissibility of illegally-obtained evidence, specifically that:
(1)	Evidence shall be excluded if it was obtained under such circumstances that its use in the proceedings would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
(2)	In determining whether evidence should be excluded under this previous section, all the circumstances surrounding the proceedings and the manner in which the evidence was obtained shall be considered, including:
(a)	the extent to which human dignity and social values were breached in obtaining the evidence;
(b)	whether any harm was inflicted on the accused or others;
(c)	whether any improper or illegal act under (a) or (6) was done wilfully or in a manner that demonstrated an inexcusable ignorance of the law;
(d)	the seriousness of any breach of the law in obtaining the evidence as compared with the seriousness of the offence with which the accused is charged;
(e)	whether there were circumstances justifying the action, such as a situation of urgency requiring action to prevent the destruction or loss of evidence.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the House for this opportunity to discuss my motion this afternoon.
In Canada, the manner in which evidence is obtained has no effect on its admissibility. This simple fact has been the subject of endless comment, debate and controversy, and this afternoon, I shall try to convince my colleagues of the advisability of amending the Canada Evidence Act to include a discretionary clause that will allow judges, in specific circumstances, to exclude evidence obtained in an improper manner.
According to the traditional concept of Common Law, evidence plays a strictly utilitarian role. Since the purpose of a criminal trial is basically to dispense justice, any evidence that is relevant, and not otherwise excluded by the rules of court proceedings, must be considered admissible by the judge, who is not concerned with the manner in which the evidence was obtained, since Common Law provides for recourse before the courts against any impropriety committed in obtaining the evidence. This is due to the fact that in criminal proceedings, the courts are obliged to provide certain procedural guarantees, while the actual investigation is not subject to the same guarantees, since the purpose of the investigation is to identify a suspect, and the purpose of court proceedings is to judge whether the suspect is or is not guilty under the law.
Yet, it cannot be denied that the proceedings and the investigation converge when the evidence is submitted. That is why some people claim either that the proceedings have priority over the investigation, which can eventually result in an exclusionary rule such as exists in the United States when the police force disregards the constitutional rights of the suspect during the investigation, or that legal ethics go beyond the proceedings to include every aspect of criminal proceedings, particularly the investigation.
That is why there are three models for the admissibility of evidence obtained by illegal means: 1) admissibility regardless of the manner in which the evidence was obtained, which is the case in Canada following the ruling in the Wray case in 1970, as well as in England, with some amendments, with regard to the law of admissions; 2) the exclusionary rule, which replaces
June 23, 1983

the truth as the pre-eminent purpose of the proceedings by another concept, namely the protection of the constitutional rights of the accused, because of which evidence obtained by illegal means must be excluded; and 3) a discretionary system which allows the judge in certain cases to reject that evidence when admitting it would be either unfair to the accused, when it is of such a nature as to bring the administration of justice into disrepute, or because of some other reason which may be recognized occasionally under various jurisdictions.
The common law of Scotland, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand follows the discretionary model. In Canada, the situation is quite complex. First, the general rule, which I mentioned earlier, stating that evidence obtained by illegal means is admissible was set by the Supreme Court in 1970 and the law has since remained unchanged, but this concept is certainly not unanimously accepted since, in the Ontario Appeals Court, Mr. Justice Aylesworth suggested a formula which has gained widespread acceptance, namely that the inherent discretion of a judge to ensure the accused of a fair trial extended to the exclusion of evidence, even though relevant, obtained by illegal means when its use would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute. This is an entirely new concept to be found nowhere else, at least under this form, in judicial precedents. While this concept was rejected by the Supreme Court, as I mentioned earlier, it was accepted by Mr. Justice Spence, who even went further when he said that such discretion should go against the Crown. Since then, various commissions have recommended that the Canadian Evidence Act include the concept of discretion to exclude evidence obtained by illegal means, and excepting the recommendations of the Ouimet Commission in 1968 which predate the Wray ruling, these recommendations include those of the Law Reform Commission, the Ontario Law Reform Commission, and finally, the Commission of Inquiry concerning certain activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, better known as the McDonald Commission, which are found in the motion now under consideration. I was saying that the situation was rather complex in Canada and this is because, irrespective of that general rule, Canadian law provides for a certain number of exceptions. First there is an exception proceeding from the Common Law concerning the admissibility of confessions made by the accused out of court. This House is aware of the general rule under which a non-voluntary statement made by the accused to an authorized official will not be accepted as evidence at the trial because the court has no means to guarantee the truthfulness of such statement. Indeed, another legal principle is that the accused cannot be coerced during the trial. Since the accused cannot be compelled to appear, the court cannot legally check the consistency between the non-voluntary previous statement and the testimony given at the trial.
A dissent that attracted considerable attention in the Rothman judgment, that of Justice Lamer who indicated that
Canada Evidence Act
beyond the voluntary aspect, he recognized an additional discretion of the judge sitting on the case to dismiss a confession even when made voluntarily when the conditions under which such a confession is made to an authorized person is tantamount to non-compliance with the principle that an accused cannot be coerced and, consequently, the administration of justice is brought into disrepute. In short, Justice Lamer was going back to the administration of justice and to the obligation for a judge to see that the whole judiciary process, not only during the proceedings but also during the investigation, operates in accordance with the minimum standards of good conduct and he extended the concept initially introduced by Justice Aylesworth to the law on confessions. That is not truly a dissent because in his charge he does not agree with the legislation now in effect but he gets the same results as the judges of the majority. However the model that he proposes is surely not part of our law. Nevertheless, it is interesting to note that the same formula recurs periodically.
Section 178.16 (2) as passed by the House in 1977 goes back to the same formula by allowing the juge sitting on the case to rule out the evidence originating from an illegal interception of private communications. In other words, where there has been illegal electronic eavesdropping and the derived evidence has been adduced, the trial judge may decide to exclude such evidence if he is satisfied that its use would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute. This is the same formula that is found in our statutes, in the Criminal Code. Unfortunately, there is no higher jurisprudence by which we could define the exact scope of that exception to the general rule as to the acceptability of improperly obtained evidence, which brings us to Section 24(2) of the Charter of Rights. Section 24(2) also allows a trial judge to exclude evidence obtained against or in spite of the rights recognized in the Charter and therefore enshrined, where its use would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute. Therefore, parallel with the general rule under which evidence may be used however obtained, here are two statutes, one of which is part of our Constitution, which introduce a quite different concept, and I am reluctant to refer to an "exception" where a concept is constitutionally enshrined. It is somewhat odd that one should suggest that this is an exception to the general rule, where the discretionary ideal takes its place and becomes part of our law.
The exclusion of evidence is justified for various considerations. First, deterrence, as this is the main reason that is generally put forward, deterrence of repugnant police practices. Under that principle, there is a specific or general standard of conduct that is either left to or imposed upon the trial judge so that he may decide where applicable to penalize

June 23, 1983
Canada Evidence Act
any abuse committed during the inquest, and through this procedural rule, namely the exclusion of evidence that could otherwise be acceptable.
This is the principle behind the American exclusion rule, known in English as the rule of the Fruit of the poisonous tree.. On the other hand, it is through an extension of the principle of the fair trial that other authorities justify the discretion to exclude improperly obtained evidence. Indeed, it is the judge's responsibility to make sure that the accused is given a fair trial. In Common Law, this was expressed by a rigid interpretation of procedural trial guarantees, although there was no intention to extend those guarantees to the inquest. For others, such as the Privy Council or more specifically the Judiciary Committee of the Privy Council, in the Sang Order of 1980, the fair trial principle was extended to documentary evidence obtained from the accused against his will, before the trial.
That is indeed an extension of justice in British trials which we Canadians do not enjoy yet. Although we might pass legislation, I do not believe we would be well advised to do so. If I may, I should like to urge Canadian judges, particularly in light of the Charter, to be more liberal in their interpretation of our principles concerning the right to confess so as to enshrine that additional element of justice which the judiciary committee of the Privy Council has acknowledged in the Sang decision.
Finally, and this relates directly to the text of the motion, an ethical conception of the role of the court in the judiciary process enables me to draw a parallel between the judiciary integrity on one hand-which does not leave any doubt-and the integrity of justice on the other-which is indeed more extensive than judiciary integrity per se.
If one endorses the principle that judiciary integrity cannot exist without the integrity of justice and the standards of behaviour which law enforcement agents must respect, one has to admit as well that a trial judge cannot be party to unacceptable investigation practices by disregarding altogether the manner in which the otherwise relevant evidence before him has been obtained. That is why the wording used in section 178.16(2) concerning wiretapping-a reprehensible activity which is strictly regulated by the Parliament of Canada and punishable by extremely severe penal and civil sanctions-and section 24(2) of the Charter of Rights, which provides for redress in cases of violations against constitutionally acknowledged or constitutionnally enshrined rights, are, in my opinion, the best answer to the double dilemma of the acceptance of a rule of admissibility so strict that it does not allow sanctioning or rather disassociating oneself from unacceptable investigation practices, on one hand, and, on the other, a rule of exclusion which is unduly restrictive, as a magistrate said in the United States: The constable blunders, the criminal goes free. And this is a delicate balancing act between opposing facets of public interest, the need to administer justice on the one hand, and the need for law enforcement agencies to use reasonable
and democratically acceptable means. It is only through discretionary powers that we can achieve this.
But there is a problem, Mr. Speaker. Neither Section 178.16(2) nor Section 24(2) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms provide a discretionary code defining the various considerations which a presiding judge should assess while carrying out his or her duties. Such a judge is instructed to dismiss all illegally-obtained evidence which might otherwise bring the administration of justice into disrepute, but he or she has no indication as to how, when, and on the basis of what criteria these discretionary powers are to be used. That is why I move that the Canada Evidence Act be amended to include a discretionary code.
I drafted my bill in line with the recommendations of the McDonald Commission. I could have drafted it in line with those of the Law Reform Commission of Canada. I could have proposed the discretionary code adopted by the Common Law of Scotland, or the one adopted by the Australian Common Law. That is not the problem.
The problem is that judges, who by now have given an interpretation of Section 24(2) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedom, do not possess the means required in order to exercise this discretion according to well defined parameters and reference marks.
I suggest it would be appropriate for us to assist the judges in carrying out this responsibility they have of eventually rejecting, in some cases, the evidence improperly obtained, and I believe that to this end, we should adopt a discretionary code which would provide these reference marks. I refer my colleagues to the text of the motion enumerating some of these considerations. Unfortunately, I do not have the time to elaborate at length on each of these points today.
I would simply like to stress one thing, Mr. Speaker. This debate is far from over. Even after Section 24(2) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms has recognized this judicial discretionary power to reject evidence improperly obtained, the proposals contained in Bill S-33, presently before the Senate, take up once again the criteria formulated in the Wray decision. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, and I will conclude my remarks with this, the Wray decision recognizes a certain amount of discretionary power to reject relevant evidence, when the effect is unduly detrimental to the accused because of its extenuated probative value. Clause 24(2) of Bill S-33 takes up textually the concept enunciated in the Wray decision. Thus, we have looped the loop. First, there is the Wray case; then 178.16(2) recognizes the discretion; Section 24(2) recognizes the discretion; and then, in Bill S-33, the new evidence code presently before Parliament, such discretion is not recognized any more.
I submit to my colleagues that it is high time we resolve this dilemma. We must recognize once and for all the judiciary discretion to reject evidence improperly obtained, when its admission would bring into disrepute the administration of
June 23, 1983

justice. And we must give the judges a discretionary code in order to give them guidance in this role.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I salute the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) for his most thoughtful address. In fairness 1 could add that he has done his thesis on the subject. He was kind enough to show me a copy of it. It has 60 pages of footnotes and many more pages of text. I indicate this in self-defence because he had many months in which to prepare and I have had less than an hour in which to prepare myself. It is not his fault; it is just that in the workings of things there has been little time to do an adequate job on a very serious subject.
The motion of the Hon. Member referred to the McDonald Commission and indicated in part:
Evidence shall be excluded if it was obtained under such circumstances that its use in the proceedings would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
He went on to indicate that in determining whether evidence should be excluded, the manner in which it was obtained should be considered, for example, including:
(a) The extent to which human dignity and social values were breached in obtaining the evidence;
Since we already have Section 24(2) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, why do we need to go further and further rigidify what is already there? In part Section 24(2) reads:
Where ... a court concludes that evidence was obtained in a manner that infringed or denied any rights or freedoms guaranteed by this Charter, the evidence shall be excluded if it is established that, having regard to all the circumstances, the admission of it in the proceedings would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
I think my concern is shared by the Hon. Member for Rosemont. Hopefully, all of us in the House agree that we do not want a situation where any evidence, no matter how heinously obtained, should be admitted into evidence. I do not think anyone wants a situation where any evidence, no matter how small the indiscretion used to obtain it, should not be admissible in evidence.
Those Members of the House who voted for the Charter of Rights and Freedoms wanted a middle ground. We did not want the absolute ban which exists in the United States. I will deal with that in a minute because it is the cause of many of the serious crime problems in the United States. Conversely, we did not want the current Canadian situation where basically if the only evidence obtainable is illegally or improperly obtained, it is admissible in the search for truth. My hon. friend referred to the Regina v. Wray case, but there have been many others.
I would like to give an example by referring to a case in the United States which will show how the other system can cause many problems. I am informed that in a drug trafficking case in New York city a warrant specified that the customs officers could look in someone's suitcase, but it did not specify that they could look for heroin. It specified other things but not
Canada Evidence Act
heroin. They opened the suitcase and found a large quantity of heroin and charged the person with importing that drug. When the case got to trial, the judge looked at the warrant and said that it did not specify heroin, and the case was dismissed. Whereas, in our system, at least up until the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, that person would have been convicted on the basis that although the evidence may have been improperly obtained, ours is a search for truth. There are remedies to go after the customs officers, but we would not see someone walking away from a charge of murder or trafficking in heroin because of the manner in which evidence was obtained. The accused can charge the police or customs officers. They should be disciplined or whatever, but the matter should stand.
Some very eloquent statements on the issue have been made by different people. I would like to quote one or two statements which appeared in the Ottawa Law Review under the article entitled, "The Admissibility of Evidence Obtained Illegally: A Comparative Analysis". The first one was by Mr. Justice Holmes, perhaps the most famous jurist of all, who said:
We have to choose, and for my part I think it a less evil that some criminals should escape than that the Government should play an ignoble part.
I think the Hon. Member for Rosemont referred to the other side of the issue in Britain, the other extreme, by indicating that "It matters not how you get the evidence; if you steal it even, it would be admissible". Another interesting quotation would be the one of Chief Justice Warren Burger of the United States Supreme Court who said in a recent case:
We can well ponder whether any community is entitled to call itself an "organized society" if it can find no way to solve the problem except by suppression of truth in the search for truth.
That was put pretty well in an article. Chief Justice Burger talked about the "reign of terror in American cities". This was about seven years ago. He asked, "Is a society redeemed if it provides massive safeguards for accused persons yet fails to provide elementary protection for decent law-abiding citizens?"
United States Appeal Court Judge Henry Friendly asked whether "guilt is not relevant". The late Justice Robert Jackson of the United States Supreme Court reminded us "that the Constitution was not intended to be a suicide pact". The same article points out that, according to a recent poll in the United States, one in three households reported to a crime survey that they exprienced some sort of crime during 1980.
Some say that the crime rate is less in Canada than in the United States. Many people believe that to be the case. I am not sure whether that is true any longer. A Gallup poll in 1982 indicated that one in four Canadians had been a victim of crime in the previous 12 months. According to the most recent crime survey by Statistics Canada, 2.8 million Criminal Code offences were reported in Canada during the calendar year 1981. Members are aware that many crimes are not reported. No one would dispute that the figure was probably much higher for 1981.

June 23, 1983
Canada Evidence Act
What does all this amount to? What I am trying to say is that there are two very real social interests: one is fighting crime, and the other is having the police act within the law. 1 have spent a number of years in court. I believe that nobody should be above the law, including the police and the Prime Minister. The law has to apply to everybody. One must ask oneself, and I am thinking primarily in the area of drugs because this is where most crime seems to occur, what can be done.
In a recent speech in Victoria by Superintendent Thomas Gardiner of the RCMP, he was quoted as saying that a cocaine charge against an accused was dropped after an officer was unable to prove reasonable cause for a search, even though the drug was found in the search.
How far do we want to go with these rights? What do we have to do to protect the rest of us who are law abiding? That is the issue. Hardened professional career criminals know that the law is there for their protection. They know that if the warrant does not say there was heroin in the suitcase of Mr. X, he will get off scot-free. If that is the case, the crime rate in Canada will very quickly become higher than in the United States.
It is not written into the United States Constitution that improperly obtained evidence should be excluded. In the case of the people v. Mapp it was held during the mid-sixties that the right against the use of illegally secured evidence was so fundamental as to be included in the due process required by the fourteenth amendment, and thus to be binding upon the state. That is what all this leads to, and I hope the Hon. Member for Rosemont agrees. I am afraid that the Supreme Court of Canada will take Section 24 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and resolutions such as this, if they are passed- and I have knowledge of some members of that court-and will say that next year, the year after or three years from now all improperly obtained evidence will be excluded. In other words, for reasons in which they believe, they will go beyond what the Hon. Member for Rosemont is asking and go to the rule that any illegally obtained evidence is inadmissible in any court in the land. That is how their counterparts operate under a charter of rights in the United States. I am afraid that we will be in the same position as is the neighbouring republic where criminals have a field day. I do not know whether you, Mr. Speaker, have ever attended a criminal case in the United States. I have, and I suspect the Hon. Member for Rosemont has as well. The system has reached the point where one wonders whether guilt or innocence is even relevant. You wonder whether safety of the public or reasonable protection of people's rights to liberty, life and protection from being mugged or raped is important.
One question seriously being asked in the United States is whether joggers-I am a jogger-should carry money. If a mugger mugs a jogger, he becomes angry if the jogger has no money. Therefore, in some parts of the United States joggers carry money.
One may laugh and say that that will never happen in Canada. I think it is fair to say that many people in the United States believe that the exclusionary rule is one of the causes of the state of affairs whereby crime has become rampant. They
have all of the rights such as liberty and pursuit of happiness, but they cannot go out at night on the streets of Detroit or many other cities. Everybody here thinks we live in a country where those rights are protected.
I believe we can go too far. The pendulum can only swing so far before your wife, my daughter and the niece of the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) cannot go out on the streets at night. People say, "By George, we have our constitutional rights in this country" and, therefore, you cannot convict Mr. Wray of murder because the weapon was found in a way that some may consider improper or illegal. Are we further ahead if we swing that far with the pendulum?
The Hon. Member for Rosemont probably thinks I am exaggerating, that this will not happen and the courts will not go that far, that they will maintain the middle ground that we have in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I remind him that the absolute ban on illegally obtained evidence was enacted by judicial legislation in the United States. Unfortunately the Hon. Member will not have time to reply later and tell us whether he disagrees, but I am afraid that that will happen under this provision in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If it does, the dope addicts and drug pushers will be happy.
Before the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was tested, over $8 billion was spent on illegal drugs in Canada in 1981. This includes $2.2 billion on heroin by 2,000 users. These figures are from the RCMP. There was $475 million spent on cocaine by 225,000 users, $5 billion on marijuana hashish and liquid hashish by three million users, one-third of them teenagers.
I should stress that most of the problems arise in the area of drug pushers, professional drug traffickers. What it comes down to is that my hon. friend and I agree that there should be discretion in the courts to exclude or include improperly obtained evidence, depending on the circumstances. We might disagree on particular cases and his criteria would, I think, attempt to maintain a balance, but I am concerned'that before many years have gone by, his proposals will be gone, the clearly stated wording in Section 24(2) will be gone, and we will find ourselves in a situation where all improperly obtained evidence is inadmissible in any court in Canada.
As crime prevention spokesman for the Official Opposition, while I am speaking as an individual, I am profoundly concerned that if that day ever comes, it will cause the crime rate to go up even higher than it already is. I am sure you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that the crime rate in Canada is already very high and getting higher with the passage of each year.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support resolution No. 94. I think that it is a very sensible, well worked out resolution. It is certainly in line with what was proposed by the Law Reform Commission. Indeed, it uses the actual wording of the recommendations of the MacDonald Commission. It is a very reasonable statement and is
June 23, 1983

an attempt to repair by legislation the very serious situation brought about by decisions made by our courts, including the Supreme Court of Canada. It follows logically from the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and, indeed, we might see it as fleshing out those proposals. Let me read from Section 24(2) of the Charter:
(2) Where, in proceedings under subsection (1), a court concludes that evidence was obtained in a manner that infringed or denied any rights or freedoms guaranteed by this Charter, the evidence shall be excluded if it is established that, having regard to all the circumstances, the admission of it in the proceedings would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
This is a very sensible Canadian middle of the road solution to a problem. Its idea is not to go whole hog as in the United States where there is an exclusionary rule that everything would automatically be excluded if there was even the merest technical infraction. Incidentally, the position taken in the United States has been greatly exaggerated in debate by suggesting that many criminals go scot-free on the basis of technicalities. It has been estimated that getting rid of the exclusionary rule would increase the rate of conviction by less than 1 per cent.
The dramatic remarks made by the previous speaker about crime on the streets requiring joggers to carry money to buy off criminals are absolutely preposterous. Of course, what is in mind here is not even an exclusionary rule but, rather, exclusionary discretion, a rule which would not even go as far as does the rule in the United States.
This resolution is in line with, and indeed is better than, the Law Reform Commission's recommendations of 1974, for the Law Reform Commission argued the matter in a backward way. It would continue the admission of illegally obtained evidence if the evidence were otherwise relevant and credible, but would give the judge discretion to depart from this, the discretion to admit "evidence obtained through a serious violation of a substantive law or fundamental right if, considering the circumstances and the gravity of the charge against the accused, the violation is the result of a deliberate voluntary act committed in bad faith, its admission would constitute a serious injustice to the accused or bring the administration of justice into disrepute."
That is a rather heavy-handed approach on the part of the Law Reform Commission, but we all know that the Law Reform Commission is desperately afraid to be on the side of reform. What we have in the resolution is the word "shall"; that if the administration of justice would be brought into disrepute, the evidence shall be disregarded. Specific guidelines are given as to what is to be weighed in the balance. The judge is directed to weigh the pros and cons, the seriousness of the offence, the seriousness of the violation of the rights of the accused, and determine accordingly.
This position is very similar to the position taken in Scotland, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand and other countries. I can do not better than to quote from a famous Scottish case, Lawrie versus Muir, a decision of Lord Cooper. "The law must strive to reconcile two highly important interests which are
Canada Evidence Act
liable to come into conflict: (a) the interest of the citizen to be protected from illegal or irregular invasions of his liberties by the authorities, and (b) the interest of the state to secure that evidence bearing upon the commission of a crime and necessary to enable justice to be done shall not be withheld from courts of law on any mere formal or technical ground. Neither of these objects can be insisted upon to the uttermost. The protection for the citizen is primarily protection for the innocent citizen against unwarranted, wrongful, and perhaps high-handed interference, and the common sanction is an action for damages .... On the other hand, the interest of the state cannot be magnified to the point of causing all the safeguards for the protection of the citizen to vanish, and of offering a positive inducement to the authorities to proceed by irregular methods."
It is not an absolute rule but a question of circumstance, and the factors to be taken into account include the following: Did the irregularity occur deliberately or accidentally? How serious is it? Is it a mere technical breach or something involving a threat to personal liberty? Was there an emergency involved in obtaining the evidence? Were those responsible for the illegal conduct police officers? How serious is the case against the accused? In fact, Scottish courts have admitted illegally obtained evidence where there is reason to believe the suspect would destroy the evidence, a rather practical approach to the problem.
The proposals of resolution No. 94 are very similar to proposals advocated by my colleague, the Attorney General for Manitoba, the Hon. Roland Penner, then acting in the capacity of a professor of law at the University of Manitoba. Professor Penner argued that it is a matter of legal and social policy that there be exclusionary discretion. Judicial integrity in the role of the courts as guardians of civil liberties is at issue, and of course it is difficult for judges to do this because of the Wray case and the Hogan case, so legislation is necessary.
Judicial discretion is already widely accepted in other matters of evidence, as we all know, so the concern over so-called unfettered discrimination, that there would be too great an element of uncertainty, can be countered by guidelines. That is precisely what the resolution before us does.
The sad fact is that violations of citizens' rights are commit-ed in the collection of evidence, and the courts have not played a role in stopping this. There have been some very bad decisions made on the part of the Supreme Court of Canada. Some of the decisions made are as bad as those made in women's equality cases, but like in women's equality cases, there have also been some dissenting opinions. I would like to read one from Mr. Justice Laskin, 1974, in Hogan. It reads:
The choice of policy here, i.e. the majority decision to accept the evidence, is to favour the social interest in the repression of crime despite the unlawful invasion of individual interests and despite the fact that the invasion is by public officers charged with law enforcement. Short of legislative direction, it might have been expected that the common law would seek to balance the competing interests by weighing the social interests in the particular case against the gravity or character of the invasion, leaving it to the discretion of the trial judge whether

June 23, 1983
Canada Evidence Act
the balance should be struck in favour of reception or exclusion of the particular evidence.
Where constitutional guarantees are concerned, the more pertinent consideration is whether those guarantees, as fundamentals of the particular society, should be at the mercy of law enforcement officers and a blind eye turned to their invasion because it is more important to secure a conviction. The contention that it is the duty of the courts to get at the truth has in it too much of the philosophy of the end justifying the means. It would equally challenge the present law as to confessions.
In effect, the argument here is for exclusionary discretion. The McDonald Commission advocated an exclusionary discretion as well on the basis of the Law Reform Commission's proposals, and certainly the McDonald Commission was very aware of the problems of illegally obtained evidence. That commission noted particularly the very bad effect of the current practice in Canada of there being no exclusion on police conduct. The fact that the courts have not thrown out illegally obtained evidence has been interpreted by the RCMP at all levels to mean that illegal evidence is acceptable.
Until now, the debate has been of a rather theoretical nature, and writers and commentators have perforce guessed at the effect of the law on police investigative attitudes and conduct. It can now be said, at least in this country and in regard to the RCMP, that the attitude of members of that force, as expounded by its most senior officers, is to regard the absence of critical comment by the judiciary as tacit approval of forms of conduct that might be unlawful .... It is in this sense that one may say that the present law has encouraged the police, quite erroneously, to infer that judicial silence implies approval of the investigative method that has been described in court.
I should like to support the resolution, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the Government will not talk it out. After all, it is a proposal, a statement of principle; it is not an Act. If parliamentary reform means anything, I think it should be possible for the House to pass matters of this sort even if they have not been introduced by a Minister.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF IMPLEMENTING RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with the first part of the motion which reads as follows:
Evidence shall be excluded if it was obtained under such circumstances that its use in the proceedings would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
In 1975 the Law Reform Commission of Canada proposed an evidence code in its first report to Parliament. In that report the Commission advocated that a judge should have a power to exclude evidence in certain circumstances. Two provisions of that code are important to us in our consideration of the motion today. Section 15 of the proposed evidence code is identical to the recommendation contained in the report of the MacDonald Commission and in the motion brought before the House today. Accordingly, I need not read it now.
in Section 16 of its proposed evidence code, the Law Reform Commission recommended a specific provision concerning the admissibility of statements, and that provision reads as follows:
A statement made by the accused to a person in authority is inadmissible if tendered by the prosecution in a criminal proceeding, unless the judge is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the statement was not made under circumstances (including the presence of threats or promises) that were likely to render the statement unreliable, or unless the accused personally or through his counsel agrees to its admission.
Nothing in this section affects the admissibility of evidence other than a statement of the accused, including evidence of any fact discovered as a result of such statement or that such facts were discovered as a result of the statement.
The legal profession in Canada did not greet the report prepared by the Law Reform Commission of Canada with much enthusiasm. As a result, the Law Reform Commission of Ontario turned its attention to the law of evidence, and subsequently published a report in 1976. In that report the Ontario Commission also recommended that a judge should have the discretion to exclude evidence is it was obtained illegally and its admission would be unfair to the opposing party, or if evidence was obtained by methods that are repugnant to the fair administration of justice. The latter part of this recommendation was expressly designed to combat what the Law Reform Commission of Ontario perceived as bad policy in the decision given by the Supreme Court of Canada in Regina v. Wray. I think this case has been referred to by all Hon. Members who have spoken on this matter.
Then in 1981, the MacDonald Commission, as it was popularly known, recommended that a legislative provision be enacted in terms identical to those proposed in Section 15 of the evidence code of the Law Reform Commission of Canada. In its report, the MacDonald Commission made a brief survey of law as it stands in Canada and in other jurisdictions, as well as a summary of arguments for and against the discretion to exclude illegally obtained evidence. The Commission expressed its support for a discretion to exclude in Clause 64 which reads as follows:
In our view, the law of Canada should, like that of Scotland and Australia, give the trial judge a discretion to exclude illegally and unfairly obtained evidence. It will be noted that we do not propose the adoption of the American rule requiring the absolute exclusion of all illegally obtained evidence. The Canadian rule should be discretionary rather than absolute, because:
(A)	The state's commitment to due process would be seriously diluted if the court in the most serious of crimes were to exclude evidence that was obtained as a result of the most trivial breaches of the laws of search. Rather than demonstrating the commitment of the law to principle, such a result would confirm in the minds of many members of the public the commitment of the law to technicality and in their minds would bring the law into disrepute. Therefore, the protection of judicial integrity and encouraging confidence in the judicial system require a discretionary rather than an absolute rule.
(B)	The rationale of deterrence ought logically to apply only to intentional breaches of the law. Generally, an absolute rule of exclusion fails to distinguish between wilful and flagrant conduct on the part of the police on the one hand, and conscientious and careful police conduct undertaken in a difficult situation, on the other. An absolute rule fails to distinguish between errors of judgment that cause no harm and those that seriously violate fundamental values. An absolute rule fails to distinguish between a minor case such as shoplifting, and a grave case such as murder. Any rule that fails to discriminate between those different factual circumstances is too blunt an instrument to achieve any of its objectives, such as the preservation of judicial integrity and the deterrence of improper or illegal police conduct.
June 23, 1983

In the six years between 1975, when the Law Reform Commission of Canada published its evidence code, and 1981, with the publication of the report of the MacDonald Commission, three law reform bodies recommended that a judge should have the power to exclude illegally obtained evidence in certain circumstances and according to certain conditions. The argument in favour of such a power found some favour with law makers at both the provincial and federal levels because the next crucial development in this area of the law came in 1982 with the proclamation of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Section 24 of the Charter provides as follows:
24. (1) Anyone whose rights or freedoms, as guaranteed by this Charter, have been infringed or denied may apply to a court of competent jurisdiction to obtain such remedy as the court considers appropriate and just in the circumstances.
(2) Where, in proceedings under subsection (1), a court concludes that evidence was obtained in a manner that infringed or denied any rights or freedoms guaranteed by this Charter, the evidence shall be excluded if it is established that, having regard to all the circumstances, the admission of it in the proceedings would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
Under Subsection 24(2), therefore, a court can exclude evidence obtained by virtue of a constitutional violation if in the court's assessment of all the circumstances, the admission of the evidence would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. This power is, of course, predicated upon a violation of constitutionally protected rights. Thus the Charter gives some broad recognition to the exclusion of illegally obtained evidence. However, Subsection 24(2) of the Charter is not the only provision of Canadian law that would allow the exclusion of evidence on the basis that its admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. In 1976 Parliament enacted a specific provision that would permit the exclusion of wiretap evidence if its admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. Subsection 178.16(2) of the Criminal Code reads as follows:
Notwithstanding Subsection (1), the judge or magistrate presiding at any proceedings may refuse to admit evidence obtained directly or indirectly as a result of information acquired by interception of a private communication that is itself inadmissible as evidence where he is of the opinion that the admission thereof would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
Let us now turn our attention to current developments in Canada. In 1977, following the report on evidence from the Law Reform Commission of Canada and the Law Reform Commission of Ontario, the Uniform Law Conference undertook, as it were, to prepare a synthesis and a Uniform Evidence Act that would be amenable to application in both the provincial and federal jurisdictions. To carry out this work, the Uniform Law Conference established a federal-provincial task force on uniform rules of evidence. The work of this task force was completed before the proclamation of the Charter. The task force made recommendations for reform in the law of evidence and tabled before the Uniform Law Conference a draft Act. In its report the task force devoted an entire chapter, Chapter 16, to illegally obtained evidence. The Uniform Evidence Act, as passed by the Uniform Law Conference in plenary session, was taken up by the Governments of Canada's
Canadian Flag
various jurisdictions. After several amendments to the Uniform Evidence Act and after extensive consultation with the Provinces, the federal Government tabled Bill S-33 in the Senate in November, 1982. The provision of the Bill that affects the admissibility of evidence is Clause 22 which reads as follows:
Relevant evidence is admissible unless it is excluded pursuant to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, this Act or any other Act or law, and evidence that is not relevant is not admissible.
The court may exclude evidence the admissibility of which is tenuous, the probative force of which is trifling in relation to the main issue and the admission of which would be gravely prejudicial to a party.
It would appear, therefore, that the Bill proceeds on the recommendation of the task force that no provision should be enacted to allow for the exclusion of illegally obtained evidence. This, indeed, was the position advocated by the federal-provincial task force, and I should like to quote a passage from that report. It reads:
The common law rule that judges should not be concerned with the propriety of the means used by a party to obtain evidence is subject to two exceptions in criminal cases: confessions and wiretap evidence. To ensure that a confession is reliable and that the accused's right to silence was not violated, the judge must inquire into whether a confession was obtained voluntarily. To protect the citizen against unauthorized wiretapping and eavesdropping the Criminal Code prohibits wiretapping or bugging unless the party obtains either the consent of a party to the communication or the authority of a court order. The Code also regulates the admissibility of such evidence in criminal proceedings. The sanctions in the Code would seem to be effective deterrents of illegal wiretapping and to make unnecessary an exclusionary provision for civil cases. The proposed discretion would require the court to speculate about the impact of admitting illegally or improperly obtained evidence upon the police and society. The role of the judge should be limited to the conduct of the trial and should not embrace these larger issues.

AN ACT REQUIRING THE CANADIAN FLAG AND THE FLAG OF THE PROVINCE TO BE FLOWN ON FEDERAL BUILDINGS MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
That Bill C-596, an Act requiring the Canadian flag and the flag of the

June 23, 1983
Canadian Flag
Province to be flown on federal buildings, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, a little over three years ago, I rose in this House to introduce this bill entitled An Act requiring the Canadian flag and the flag of the Province to be flown on federal buildings. I would like to remind my colleagues of the comments I made at that time. It was on May 21, 1980, the day after the Quebec referendum. I then said the following:
Madam Speaker, I am very proud the day after a large majority of Quebecers have expressed their will to remain in the Canadian federation to introduce this bill to provide for the flying of the Canadian flag and the flag of the province on federal buildings.
I also said:
Madam Speaker, Canadians from Quebec have rediscovered yesterday that they are proud of flying both the Canadian and the Quebec flags together. Given the spirit that prevails today in this House-
I asked for unanimous consent to proceed without debate with all stages of this Bill. I had consulted the then Leader of the Official Opposition, the Right Hon. Member for Yellow-head (Mr. Clark), the Leader of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), and the Leader of my own party (Mr. Trudeau), and ail three had given their consent. At the last minute, one of my colleagues, unaware of these negotiations, rushed into the House to object, and he was the only Member to oppose this motion. That is why this Bill is still on the order paper three years later.
I hope that today, my colleagues on all sides of the House, and particularly in my own Party, will do everything in their power to allow this bill to proceed through all stages with unanimous consent before we adjourn.
Mr. Speaker, all my Quebec colleagues and myself fought against the concept of separation at the time of the May 20, 1980 referendum. I would like to remind my colleagues what the supporters of separation were doing at that time. PQ members were going all over Quebec carrying the Quebec flag, which had become the symbol of Quebec separation and independence. As for us, supporters of federalism, we went all over the Province with both the Canadian and the Quebec flags. That is the symbol that prevailed at the referendum, which was won by federalist Quebecers by 60 per cent against 40 per cent.
1 would like the House to reflect for a few moments on the fact that very soon, perhaps within a year, the Parti Quebecois will hold another referendum or a provincial election on Quebec sovereignty. For my part, as I am convinced that, as a French-speaking Quebecer, I belong in Canada, I would like the Canadian Bag and the provincial flag, the flag of my Province, to be flown on federal buildings, especially in Quebec, as a token of our attachment and our sense of belonging to this country.
This very short and simple Bill contains three Clauses. The first Clause provides the following:
The Canadian flag and the flag of each of the provinces and of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories shall be flown from the Parliament buildings situated in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, on Canada Day next week, all these flags will be flown side by side on Parliament Hill in front of the Centre Block. All the visitors to our national capital city will be happy to see the flag of their own province flying on Parliament Hill. Unfortunately, it is only for a week and then the flags are removed. I still wonder why. In a country such as Canada which is a federation of ten provinces and two territories, I wonder why those flags are flown during only one week in the year when they should be flown all year round on Parliament Hill. It is the first Clause of my Bill.
The second Clause of my Bill reads as follows:
The Canadian flag shall be flown on all buildings owned by the Crown in right of Canada as well as on all buildings occupied by federal services.
We know that in all Provinces, many rented buildings are occupied by federal services. This legislation would compel the owners of those buildings to fly the Canadian flag and that of the relevant Province. Besides, several provinces if not all, except Quebec, are already flying on their own provincial buildings both the Canadian and the provincial flags. Unfortunately, in Quebec this is not done. However, I think that as federal Members we should set the example and fly both flags on our own buildings.
The third Clause merely states the following:
The Governor in Council may by regulation define "building" for the purposes of this Act.
This is a very simple Bill which has a great symbolic importance especially in Quebec. As I said a few moments ago, we will soon have another battle to fight in Quebec over the issue of independance or attachment to the Canadian federation. I am convinced beforehand that the Parti Quebecois will launch its campaign by flying the Quebec flag as a symbol and again as federal Members of Quebec, we will fight with both flags in both hands. Why not legislate this dual attachment and this dual symbol throughout the country and not just in Quebec?
I will not say anything more, Mr. Speaker, because there is very little time left until adjournment, but I hope my colleagues on both sides of the House, particularly on this side, will shorten their speeches so that before we adjourn we may ask with unanimous consent that the House go through all stages of this Bill to put this legislation on our statute books so that we will be able as soon as possible to fly both the Canadian flag and the provincial flag on all federal buildings in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Comtois) for bringing in Bill C-596. I think that all of us who are at the
June 23, 1983

federal or provincial level of legislative activities are interested in the symbolism of flags and feel that we bear some responsibility to consider proposals such as the one brought in by the Hon. Member. At first glance, I do not see much objection to the proposal, although I note that the description of the Bill reads: "An Act requiring the Canadian flag and the flag of the Province to be flown on federal buildings". That seems to be mandatory, as it is stated there. However, when one goes through into the reading of the Act itself, one finds that Clause 2(2) states:
The flag of the Province or the territory in which the building is situate may also be flown on such buildings.
I simply detected a discrepancy. I am not sure whether the Hon. Member's real intention is that the flag shall be flown as the title seems to suggest, if I am using the right terms in describing the heading of the entire Act. However, I am just wondering whether or not the Government's real intention is that it will be mandatory for the Provinces to fly the provincial flags.
The only other problem I see probably lies in Clause 1 of the proposed Bill. 1 certainly have no objections to the philosophy of having the provincial flags flying on the Parliament buildings here in Ottawa. I see some merit in it, although it might be overdoing a good thing, in a way. It is certainly appropriate to have the Canadian flag flying here. I know that none of us would dispute that. I just wonder how it would look and the logistics that would be involved in flying the 12 other flags. I dare say that it could be done. 1 see the wisdom of it on ceremonial occasions such as we have had when the monarch or other people have visited. Then we want to have the flags of all our Provinces and of Canada displayed at the same time.
I think the Hon. Member for Terrebonne was perhaps suggesting that we recognize our flags in that way all the time, not just on special occasions. 1 am not so much arguing against it as I am simply raising the logistical question as to how we will fly those extra flags.
Therefore, I commend the Hon. Member for bringing the Bill before us for consideration. Perhaps he cannot, by the rules of the House, reply to my inquiry about the apparent conflict I see in what we have in front of us. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in the debate on this Bill because it was introduced by my colleague from Terrebonne (Mr. Comtois) in 1980. In my opinion, it was fitting that he introduced it the day after we won the referendum, when we Canadians of the Province of Quebec were reassured about the intentions of Canadians in that province who were anxious to remain Canadians and continue to live as such.
Canadian Flag
I am all the more pleased as I share his views on the absence of the Canadian flag on our provincial institutions, such as schools and halls of justice which are the responsibility of the Province of Quebec, and all other Government buildings which belong to the province. I think that as long as the present Quebec Government continue to refuse to fly the Canadian flag, it will be denying Canadians in that province the right to show and affirm that they belong to this great country. I think that is unacceptable. That is why I want to reassure my colleague and tell him that I support his Bill. If it is not adopted this afternoon, it will be soon, because sometimes the Government takes a little while to understand the will of Canadians. Perhaps this is a striking example of the heartfelt desire of Canadians to see the flag of their country on all Government buildings of the Province of Quebec.
As to the possibility of flying the flags of all provinces on Government buildings throughout Canada, I think that could be the subject of a debate. I am not sure I would like to see the flag . . . Perhaps there is a place near the Centre Block where the flags of the provinces and the territories might be flown.
In any event, I fully agree with my colleague from Terrebonne when he talks about the flag of the Province of Quebec.
I should like to remind the House that this blue and white flag has had an official status for a long time, for it was Queen Victoria who in 1868, granted the province of Quebec this blue flag with three white fleurs-de-lis. Even then, Quebec residents used to consider this flag as the true French-Canadian emblem, and I strongly support the Hon. Member for Terrebonne when he says that this flag cannot be identified with a political party, since it was granted to the province of Quebec in 1868, a long time before 1976.
He is perfectly right on this, and he can truly say that we are proud of our flag; I think that it is quite proper that we should be dealing with this issue on this day, the 23rd of June, the eve of St. John the Baptist Day, the day when French-Canadians everywhere celebrate their patron saint who has always been a source of inspiration to us, French Canadians, born and raised in the province of Quebec, together with other Canadians not necessarily of French descent but who are nevertheless good Canadians who have contributed to the good of our society and the economic development of our province.
I wish to say again to the Hon. Member for Terrebonne that I fully support his bill and that I hope, should it not go through today, that it will be passed in the near future, and I am looking forward to the day when this Canadian flag, which thrills the souls of all Canadians who can be proud of it, will fly over all government buildings in the province of Quebec.

June 23, 1983
Canadian Flag
I would also like to join my colleagues from Terrebonne (Mr. Comtois) and Labelle (Mr. Dupras) in discussing this legislation that has come in for second reading today. I would like to commend the Hon. Member for Terrebonne for introducing that Bill after the referendum campaign, and I feel we should hasten to pass it, because I feel it is mere political meanness not to have in this country two masts for flying first the symbol of Canadian unity, the Maple Leaf, and, second, the flag of each province. I feel this would simply be a sign of unity and pride, since there would be no contradiction between the two. We all know very well Gilles Vigneault's song "My Country is Winter". It is a factor of unity for this country to have a hard winter climate from South to North, from North to South, from East to West and Mgr. Savard has written quite an extraordinary poem entitled "My country" which closes with these words: "Happy the nations that get on well". It is my view that putting both flags side by side would simply show that the two founding groups, the French-speaking and the English-speaking, should be but one within this country, this Canada.
Of course, in Quebec the problem has been harder to experience because there is a political war going on. But despite all this, Quebecers made their choice in 1980, even though the question seemed and was in fact biased. All Quebecers are proud of their flag, and that includes the Members in this House who represent not only Quebecers but also the French Canadians, but more so those who live in Quebec. It is my view that nobody who comes here in this House has any intention of giving up anything. It is just the opposite, because when we come here we try to enhance the pride of the Quebecers and promote it from sea to sea. It is important that this be stressed.
The goal pursued by the Hon. Member for Terrebonne is indeed to stress this. There is nothing as interesting as landing at Dorval Airport and seeing federal land with both flags flying side by side, and I would even say that municipal flags should also be flown. In Quebec City, at Laval University, we see a perfect example of a trilogy in completeness. There is a triangle, with a mast at each apex, and there we have the Canadian flag, the Quebec flag and the University flag, and to whatever side one may turn there is always one of them in the center.
Therefore nobody seeks the central spot because it is a perfect triangle. In Quebec as in this Chamber, we somewhat act as missionaries because we have to explain mysteries. In religion, you have the mystery of the Trinity. In politics duality must often be explained. Thus, if only we could come back to the good old triangle which would give us a perfect base, very much like in mathematics where the triangle is the perfect form for the proper distribution of weights, everybody would be proud, including municipal governments. Everyone knows perfectly well that in current debates, mention is often made
that each level of government should guard its autonomy. We still can see instances in Quebec where as a result of government legislation , municipal authorities cannot receive federal funds. These debates may be seen as constitutional debates, but what the people of Quebec, of Ontario, of Manitoba want is to be able to keep a larger share of their tax revenues in their province.
Therefore I believe that the suggestion made by our colleague, the Hon. Member for Terrebonne, seconded by the Hon. Member for Labelle certainly deserves recognition and should be implemented without delay. I believe that when amendments are before the committee I think that one dealing with a mast for municipal governments should be moved. As a matter of fact quite often, when one refers to two flags, it is as though a choice had to be made between the two which in fact is never the case. You don't take away, you add instead, which I think is the important point. However, I find this quite difficult to explain to our constituents because we tend to refer to famous examples while we should think in more simpler terms, such as a family with the father, the mother and the child. There is never a choice to be made among them. A family is a sum of its members gathered in the same entity, just as you have a country made up of districts, municipalities and provinces.
The bill is quite welcomed and I support it fully. It is too bad Mr. Speaker, that we did not get it passed more rapidly and in that respect I think that Canadians have every right to complain when they see governments move so slowly. It is a little bit embarrassing to see such a simple and well balanced bill trigger so much debate. I believe we should speed up the process in this Chamber.
Perhaps the Hon. Member opposite was right a moment ago when he pointed out a slight difference when we say the flag should be required to be displayed, while the various clauses provide that it is merely desirable, that the Governor in Council may allow the flag to be displayed. I think we should simply try to standardize the formulation to ensure that there would be no contradiction. However, deep down, all we are asking for in this bill is that the Canadian flag as well as the flags of Ontario, Quebec and so on be equal everywhere, without one of them replacing another but instead, one adding to the greatness of the other. It is very interesting when we visit places like British Columbia or Newfoundland to see the Canadian flag everywhere and to come back home to see once more the Canadian flag, but this time accompanied by the provincial flag. I suggest one should try to the utmost to avoid such flag wars. These symbols are supposed to be a factor of unity while too often they are viewed as a factor of division. These are important aspects and I believe we should think about them.
More and more, Mr. Speaker, one can see, coming out of the economic crisis we have been through, an incredible tendency for Canadians to turn to the central Government in order to
June 23, 1983

benefit from equal revenue everywhere. One can see federal buildings being constructed in greater number in the province of Quebec as well as other provinces, and I can see a stronger federal presence in the Maritime Provinces. I believe the federal Government should not be visible alone. It is important that the federal Government be visible together with provincial Governments, with each separate entity in every province, since that is what makes for the greatness of this country. It would be desirable that the provinces do likewise and fly the Canadian colours together with their own over all provincial buildings. It would not shock anyone. It is simply a matter of common sense.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by saying that I will probably introduce amendments in committee to make sure that there are also flagpoles for municipalities. Indeed it is fine to be proud of one's country and one's province, but one should also be proud of one's municipality. It is only when we can be proud of all three of them that the great unity problem is solved.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to congratulate my colleagues, the Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Comtois), the Hon. Member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Maltais) who has just spoken regarding Bill C-596, an Act requiring the Canadian flag and the flag of the Province to be flown on federal buildings. This Act would require the Canadian flag, the flag of each Province and the flag of the Yukon and Northwest Territories to be flown from the Parliament buildings here in Ottawa. It also calls for the Canadian flag and the flag of the Province or territory where a federal building is situated to be flown on such buildings.
As I have mentioned, I applaud the intent of this Bill which I know is based on the premise that flying the flags in such a manner will indicate the complementarity of both levels of Government in the lives of all Canadians.
I must point out, however, that there are several problems which require consideration before proceeding in such a manner. First, there is the matter of identity. For example, Canadians who are looking for services of the Government of Canada know that those services are located in buildings flying the Canadian flag. If provincial flags are also flown, confusion can arise as to exactly what kind of services are being provided in that building, whether they are federal or provincial. I
Canadian Flag
believe that there should be visibility for services provided to Canadians by their national Government. The flying of the Canadian flag only on buildings owned by the Crown is one way of contributing to that necessary degree of visibility.
I think we should also consider what the Parliament buildings would look like with ten provincial flags and two territorial flags as well as the Canadian flag. I suggest that such a display would detract from the majesty of the Canadian flag flying in its solitary splendour atop the Peace Tower.
I would remind Members that a short distance from Parliament Hill is an area where all the provincial flags are flown- the Garden of Provinces. I feel that this is the appropriate place to display these flags. We should also remember that on all ceremonial occasions such as the proclamation of the Constitution last year or of Canada Day, we proudly fly the flags of Canada's Provinces and Territories at suitable locations.
I think we also must consider that it is not solely within the purview of the national Government to determine whether provincial flags should be flown along with the Canadian flag on federal buildings. I think it is important to determine the stand of the various provincial Governments and the territorial Governments on this issue. I believe the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) perhaps referred to some concerns along these same lines.
How many Provinces might agree with this type of suggestion? Surely provincial Governments also have a say in how their provincial flags are to be flown. It may be that some Provinces would not welcome the confusion of provincial flags flying from buildings owned by the Government of Canada.
I could go on but I believe that my time is up. I would certainly recommend to the House that while this suggestion is worth-while, there still needs to be much thought and consideration given to it. Again, I would like to compliment the Hon. Member for Terrebonne for bringing this private members' Bill to our attention for our consideration.

Order, please! As it is now 6 p.m., pursuant to the order adopted on Thursday, June 16, 1983, and the provisions of Standing Order 2(2), the House stands adjourned until Monday morning at eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 2(1).
At 6 p.m., the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.

Monday, June 27, 1983
